# Exercise 2.3 — Cleaning and encoding {#sec-cleaning}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## 25–30 minutes, R first
Work in R. Each task has a Python tab if you want to see the same thing in
`pandas`, but you only need to complete it in one language.
:::

## Objectives

By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

- say why a variable being categorical does not mean it should be encoded;
- group rare categories and measure what that does to the number of columns;
- find missing values that are not recorded as missing, and explain which
  convention is the most dangerous;
- tell a data-entry error from a genuine extreme, and treat them differently;
- derive BMI from height and weight, and see errors in the inputs propagate
  into it.

## The extract

`clinic_extract.csv` is 180 patients from a group of GP practices, with a
binary `diabetes` outcome. It is a realistic extract, which is to say it has
problems. Your job in this exercise is to find them.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)
library(fastDummies)

gp <- read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(gp)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
gp_py = pd.read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Task 1 — Should we one-hot encode everything? {#sec-encode-everything}

A model needs numbers, so categorical variables have to become numbers
somehow. One-hot encoding gives each category its own 0/1 column.

Take the **first 10 patients** and encode two categorical columns:
`patient_id` and `GP_practice`. Then count what you got.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
first10 <- gp |> slice_head(n = ______)

encoded <- dummy_cols(
  first10,
  select_columns = c("patient_id", "______"),
  remove_selected_columns = TRUE
)

sum(str_detect(names(encoded), "^patient_id_"))    # how many?
sum(str_detect(names(encoded), "^GP_practice_"))   # and how many?
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the number of rows asked for. The second is the other column
you are encoding.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
first10 <- gp |> slice_head(n = 10)

encoded <- dummy_cols(
  first10,
  select_columns = c("patient_id", "GP_practice"),
  remove_selected_columns = TRUE
)

sum(str_detect(names(encoded), "^patient_id_"))
sum(str_detect(names(encoded), "^GP_practice_"))
```

Ten patients, ten columns from `patient_id` — one per person. Each column is 1
for exactly one patient and 0 for everyone else, so it can only ever identify
that individual. On the full 180 rows it would produce 180 columns, each one
useless to a model that has to generalise to patient 181.

`GP_practice` produced a handful, and each of those columns describes something
several patients share.
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

first10 = gp_py.head(______)
enc = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False)
out = enc.fit_transform(first10[["patient_id", "______"]])

names = enc.get_feature_names_out(["patient_id", "GP_practice"])
print(sum(n.startswith("patient_id") for n in names))
print(sum(n.startswith("GP_practice") for n in names))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Same two blanks as the R version: the row count, and the other column.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

first10 = gp_py.head(10)
enc = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False)
out = enc.fit_transform(first10[["patient_id", "GP_practice"]])

names = enc.get_feature_names_out(["patient_id", "GP_practice"])
print(sum(n.startswith("patient_id") for n in names))
print(sum(n.startswith("GP_practice") for n in names))
```
:::
:::
:::

### Think about it

- Why does encoding `patient_id` give one column per patient?
- Those columns are perfectly valid numbers. What can a model do with them?
- Should an identifier ever be a predictor?

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The point
Being categorical does not make a variable worth encoding. An identifier is
categorical and carries no information that transfers to a new patient —
encoding it buys 180 columns of nothing. Decide what a variable *means* before
deciding what to do with it.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Task 2 — Rare categories

Now look at `GP_practice` across all 180 patients. Count the practices, plot
them, and see what encoding costs before and after you group the rare ones.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
gp |> ______(GP_practice, sort = TRUE)

gp |>
  count(GP_practice) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(GP_practice, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "patients")

before <- ncol(dummy_cols(gp, select_columns = "GP_practice",
                          remove_selected_columns = TRUE))

gp <- gp |>
  mutate(GP_practice = fct_lump_min(factor(GP_practice),
                                    min = ______,
                                    other_level = "Other"))

after <- ncol(dummy_cols(gp, select_columns = "GP_practice",
                         remove_selected_columns = TRUE))
c(before = before, after = after)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the dplyr verb that tabulates a column. The second is the
threshold — practices with fewer than this many patients get grouped.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
gp |> count(GP_practice, sort = TRUE)

gp |>
  count(GP_practice) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(GP_practice, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "patients")

before <- ncol(dummy_cols(gp, select_columns = "GP_practice",
                          remove_selected_columns = TRUE))

gp <- gp |>
  mutate(GP_practice = fct_lump_min(factor(GP_practice),
                                    min = 10,
                                    other_level = "Other"))

after <- ncol(dummy_cols(gp, select_columns = "GP_practice",
                         remove_selected_columns = TRUE))
c(before = before, after = after)

levels(gp$GP_practice)
sum(gp$GP_practice == "Other")
```

Three practices had fewer than 10 patients. Note where they went: the extract
*already had* an `Other` category, and `fct_lump_min()` merged them into it
rather than inventing a second one. Check the level list — there is one `Other`,
not two.
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
print(gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts())

counts = gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts()
rare = counts[counts < ______].index
gp_py["GP_practice"] = gp_py["GP_practice"].where(
    ~gp_py["GP_practice"].isin(rare), "______"
)
print(gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts())
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The threshold is the same as the R version. The second blank is the label
everything rare is folded into — and it already exists in the data, so use it
exactly as spelled.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
print(gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts())

counts = gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts()
rare = counts[counts < 10].index
gp_py["GP_practice"] = gp_py["GP_practice"].where(
    ~gp_py["GP_practice"].isin(rare), "Other"
)
print(gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts())
```
:::
:::
:::

### Think about it

- The threshold was 10. What is that number a statement about — the data, or
  your willingness to estimate an effect from a handful of rows?
- What did you lose by grouping?
- If an 80/20 split put all 5 patients from one practice in the test set, what
  would that column be worth in training?

## Task 3 — Find and fix the messy data

This is the investigation. Nobody is going to tell you what is wrong with this
extract; find out.

### Part A — Missing values that are not missing

Start by asking what type each column came in as, and what the unparseable
values actually are.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
sapply(gp, class)
sum(is.na(gp))               # how much is missing, apparently?

# Look at what is actually in the suspect columns
for (col in c("height_cm", "weight_kg", "systolic_BP", "smoking_status")) {
  cat("\n", col, ":\n")
  print(head(sort(table(gp[[col]], useNA = "ifany"), decreasing = TRUE), ______))
}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The blank just limits how many of the commonest values you print — 8 is plenty.
Read the output before going on.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
sapply(gp, class)
sum(is.na(gp))

for (col in c("height_cm", "weight_kg", "systolic_BP", "smoking_status")) {
  cat("\n", col, ":\n")
  print(head(sort(table(gp[[col]], useNA = "ifany"), decreasing = TRUE), 8))
}
```

Five conventions are in use: `unknown`, `?`, `not recorded`, `N/A`, `-999`, and
genuinely empty cells. `is.na()` sees only the empty ones.
:::
:::
:::

Now convert them. `na_if()` replaces one value with `NA`; `across()` applies it
to several columns at once.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
na_codes <- c("unknown", "?", "not recorded", "______", "-999")

gp <- gp |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ if_else(as.character(.x) %in% na_codes,
                                        NA_character_, as.character(.x)))) |>
  mutate(across(c(age, height_cm, weight_kg, systolic_BP), ______))

sum(is.na(gp))        # compare with the count you got before
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the fourth code in the list you just printed. The second is
the function that turns a character column into a numeric one.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
na_codes <- c("unknown", "?", "not recorded", "N/A", "-999")

gp <- gp |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ if_else(as.character(.x) %in% na_codes,
                                        NA_character_, as.character(.x)))) |>
  mutate(across(c(age, height_cm, weight_kg, systolic_BP), as.numeric)) |>
  mutate(diabetes = as.integer(diabetes))

sum(is.na(gp))
colSums(is.na(gp))
```

The missing count jumps once the codes are recognised. Everything that was
hiding as text is now a real `NA`, and the four measurement columns are numeric.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## `-999` is the dangerous one
The text codes are rude but honest: they force the column to character, so R
warns and Python raises the moment you try to average it. You find out.

`-999` is a number. `systolic_BP` loads as a perfectly ordinary numeric column
and its mean comes out at **73.6 mmHg** instead of 131.7 — a figure that would
mean your average patient was in shock. No error. No warning. Nothing but a
wrong answer, and you only catch it by knowing what blood pressure looks like.

Sentinel values like `-999`, `0` for a missing date, or `99` for "not asked" are
the most dangerous convention in clinical data for exactly this reason.
:::

### Part B — Inconsistent labels

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
table(gp$sex)
table(gp$smoking_status, useNA = "ifany")

gp <- gp |>
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      str_to_lower(str_trim(sex)) %in% c("male", "m")   ~ "Male",
      str_to_lower(str_trim(sex)) %in% c("female", "______") ~ "Female"
    ),
    smoking_status = str_to_sentence(str_trim(
      str_replace(smoking_status, "ex smoker", "ex-smoker")))
  ) |>
  mutate(smoking_status = str_remove(smoking_status, " smoker$"))

table(gp$sex)
table(gp$smoking_status, useNA = "ifany")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The blank is the one-letter abbreviation for the second category. Lower-casing
alone would fix `male` but not `M`, which is why `case_when()` lists both forms.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
table(gp$sex)
table(gp$smoking_status, useNA = "ifany")

gp <- gp |>
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      str_to_lower(str_trim(sex)) %in% c("male", "m")   ~ "Male",
      str_to_lower(str_trim(sex)) %in% c("female", "f") ~ "Female"
    ),
    smoking_status = str_to_sentence(str_trim(
      str_replace(smoking_status, "ex smoker", "ex-smoker")))
  ) |>
  mutate(smoking_status = str_remove(smoking_status, " smoker$"))

table(gp$sex)
table(gp$smoking_status, useNA = "ifany")
```

Six spellings of sex become two; four spellings of smoking status become three.
Nothing was dropped — the counts still add to 180 minus the genuinely missing.
:::
:::
:::

### Part C — Errors and extremes

Plot first. An implausible value is easier to see than to define.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| fig-height: 2.4
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
gp |>
  select(age, height_cm, weight_kg, systolic_BP) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "______") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The columns are on wildly different scales, so each panel needs its own axis.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.4
gp |>
  select(age, height_cm, weight_kg, systolic_BP) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Three things should stand out: an age far beyond any human lifespan, a weight
no patient has, and a cluster of heights near zero.
:::
:::
:::

Now decide what to do about each one. **The decisions are not the same.**

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
gp |> filter(age > 120 | weight_kg > 300 | height_cm < 3) |>
  select(patient_id, age, height_cm, weight_kg)

gp <- gp |>
  mutate(
    # Recoverable: a height in metres is unambiguous, so fix it
    height_cm = if_else(height_cm < 3, height_cm * ______, height_cm),
    # Not recoverable: we cannot know the intended value, so admit it
    age       = if_else(age > 120, NA_real_, age),
    weight_kg = if_else(weight_kg > 300, ______, weight_kg)
  )

summary(gp$height_cm)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank converts metres to centimetres. The second is what you set a
value to when you know it is wrong but cannot know what it should be.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
gp |> filter(age > 120 | weight_kg > 300 | height_cm < 3) |>
  select(patient_id, age, height_cm, weight_kg)

gp <- gp |>
  mutate(
    height_cm = if_else(height_cm < 3, height_cm * 100, height_cm),
    age       = if_else(age > 120, NA_real_, age),
    weight_kg = if_else(weight_kg > 300, NA_real_, weight_kg)
  )

summary(gp$height_cm)
```

Three different treatments for three problems:

- **The heights in metres are corrected**, because `1.61` can only have meant
  `161`. Nothing is guessed.
- **The age of 250 becomes `NA`**, because it could have been 25, 50, or a
  mistyped date of birth. Inventing a value would be worse than admitting
  ignorance.
- **The 800 kg becomes `NA`** for the same reason.

What we did *not* do is remove every point outside 1.5×IQR. Look at the
boxplots again: plenty of genuinely heavy and genuinely light patients sit out
there, and they are real. A statistical outlier is a claim about a
distribution; a data-entry error is a claim about a keyboard.
:::
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Task 4 — Feature engineering: BMI

Height and weight are now clean. BMI is more clinically useful than either on
its own, and it is one line to compute.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| fig-height: 2.4
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
gp <- gp |>
  mutate(BMI = weight_kg / (height_cm / ______)^2)

summary(gp$BMI)

ggplot(gp, aes(x = BMI)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(y = NULL)

sum(is.na(gp$______))   # how many patients have no BMI, and why?
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
BMI is kg/m², and height is in centimetres. The last blank is the column you
just made.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.4
gp <- gp |>
  mutate(BMI = weight_kg / (height_cm / 100)^2)

summary(gp$BMI)

ggplot(gp, aes(x = BMI)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(y = NULL)

sum(is.na(gp$BMI))
```

A plausible distribution, and a number of patients with no BMI at all. BMI is
missing whenever *either* height or weight is missing, so the gaps in the two
inputs combine — more patients lack a BMI than lack either measurement on its
own.
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
gp_py["BMI"] = gp_py["weight_kg"] / (gp_py["height_cm"] / ______) ** 2
print(gp_py["BMI"].describe())
print(gp_py["BMI"].isna().sum())
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
#| eval: false
gp_py["BMI"] = gp_py["weight_kg"] / (gp_py["height_cm"] / 100) ** 2
print(gp_py["BMI"].describe())
print(gp_py["BMI"].isna().sum())
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## What would have happened if you had skipped Part C
Suppose you had computed BMI *before* fixing the heights. A patient recorded as
`1.61` metres instead of `161` centimetres gives

$$\frac{84.3}{(1.61/100)^2} \approx 325{,}000$$

against a plausible range of roughly 16 to 44. One keystroke in an input column
became a value five thousand times too large in a derived one — and if you had
gone straight to a model, nothing would have stopped you.

Errors propagate into derived features, and they get harder to recognise the
further they travel from the thing that was mistyped.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Reflection

1. Encoding `patient_id` produced one column per patient. Name another variable
   in a clinical extract that is categorical and should not be encoded.
2. Grouping rare practices cut the encoded columns from 16 to 13. What would
   you say to a colleague who proposes grouping anything under 50?
3. The text codes caused a loud failure and `-999` a silent one. Which would you
   rather inherit, and what would you add to your loading code to catch the
   silent kind?
4. You corrected the heights but set the impossible age to `NA`. Write the rule
   that separates those two decisions in one sentence.

## Stretch

### Stretch 1 — A reusable audit
Write a function that takes any data frame and reports, for each column: its
type, the number of genuine `NA`s, any values matching common sentinel
conventions (`-999`, `-99`, `9999`), and the number of distinct values that
differ only by case or surrounding whitespace. Run it on the raw file and see
whether it finds everything you found by hand.

### Stretch 2 — Which error mattered?
Compute the mean BMI three ways: with the metre-heights left uncorrected, with
those rows dropped, and with them corrected as you did above. The three answers
are very different. Which of the three would a careless analysis most likely
report, and why is it the worst of the three?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where this leaves you

Save your cleaned data — @sec-imputation picks it up exactly here.

```{r}
#| eval: false
write_csv(gp, "gp_patients_cleaned.csv")
```

The extract is now internally consistent: one spelling per category, rare
practices grouped, impossible values either corrected or admitted as missing,
and BMI derived from measurements you have checked.

What it is **not** is complete. Height, weight, blood pressure and smoking
status all still have gaps, and this exercise deliberately did not fill a single
one — correcting a value you can infer is cleaning, but inventing a value you
cannot is a different decision with different consequences.

> **Our data are cleaner, but some measurements are still missing. What should
> we do with them?**

That is @sec-imputation.
